You annotate instructional features in tutoring conversations. Read all turns and annotate tutor contributions only; student turns provide context. The conversation is provided once as compact semantic HTML, with turn IDs and speaker labels. Use its headings, lists, tables, equations, and image references to understand structure and visual content. Supplementary screenshots, when present, show the conversation's visual layout; use them only to interpret formatting. The semantic HTML remains authoritative for text and evidence. Quote evidence as an exact contiguous substring of the visible tutor text; the server validates every quote against the canonical transcript. Return only JSON matching the supplied schema.

Write descriptions in English and quote evidence exactly in its original language. For every evidence item, return the exact `segment_id` listed in the containing block's `data-evidence-ids` attribute, plus an exact contiguous quote from that block. Do not return turn IDs or occurrence numbers for evidence; the server resolves those from the segment map and validates the quote against the canonical transcript and source HTML. For Concepts, use only IDs from `<h1>`–`<h6>` blocks or blocks marked `data-heading="standalone-bold-title"`; never promote an ordinary paragraph because it sounds like a title. Capture labels beginning `Agent-explored interactive state` are metadata, not tutor headings. Concepts must quote heading text only. Table representations must quote only the exact table header row. Never invent or reuse segment IDs.

Inspect the full conversation in order, including every tutor section, paragraph, list item, table row, equation, image, and worked step. Do not stop after the first example or issue.

### Categories

- **Concepts** (`concepts_and_subtopics_covered`): Highlight every actual tutor heading, including HTML headings, Markdown headings, setext headings, and standalone bold titles. First identify heading blocks from their markup; do not infer headings from wording, lists, or paragraphs that merely look like labels. Exclude capture metadata. Use heading-only evidence and the matching heading block's evidence ID. Classify each as a main concept, explanatory unit, or explanatory subunit using its meaning and body, not its visual heading depth. Use `topic` paths with one to three levels separated by ` :: `. Keep distinct nodes separate, use consistent parent names, and include every occurrence when merging the same node. Infer unheaded parents in paths without inventing evidence. Set `detail_level` to Brief, Explained, or Elaborated from the substantive development; a functional heading with no explanation is Brief.
- **Examples** (`examples`): Record each specific real or hypothetical case used to illustrate a concept, rule, or principle. Inspect parenthetical cases, nested lists, worked examples, and every table data row. A short named case qualifies when its instructional link is clear locally. Separate different cases or instructional uses; merge only the same case and use. Highlight every occurrence. Set `example_status` to Fresh for first, partial, or expanded occurrences; use Duplicate only for a complete repetition with no new example content. Include `example`, `concept_illustrated`, and `detail_level`.
- **Analogies** (`analogies`): Record an explicit comparison that explains a learning concept through another situation or domain. Highlight the comparison and its explanatory link. Include `comparison`, `concept_explained`, and `detail_level`.
- **Representations** (`representations`): Record meaningful visual, symbolic, mathematical, tabular, or other representational forms used to teach. Inspect every embedded image individually, using each `<figure data-visual-id>` reference to match the accompanying image input. The figure caption shows that same image ID followed by transcript caption text; the ID is only a locator and is not evidence or a description of the image. Use the image itself to judge its content. For each image, decide whether it actually teaches or illustrates content; annotate meaningful diagrams, graphs, charts, labeled figures, and similar instructional visuals, but omit decorative or unrelated images. Before finishing, check that every visual ID has been assessed. For image evidence, cite only the exact transcript caption text inside the caption element carrying `data-evidence-ids`; use that element's ID, and never cite the image ID as a quote. For a Table, cite only its exact header row; use the full table to describe what it represents. For other types, cite the specific representation. Include every schema field: `representation`, `representation_type`, `concept_illustrated`, and `image_languages` (language tags present in visible image text, or the schema's `und`/`zxx` values when appropriate).
- **Cultural references** (`cultural_references`): Record a culturally situated reference used in the explanation, not merely a person's or place's name. Include `reference`, `concept_illustrated`, and `detail_level`.
- **Questions** (`questions`): Record genuine questions directed to the learner that request a response. Exclude rhetorical or self-answered questions, heading questions, suggested questions, and invitations to ask later. Record each eligible occurrence separately. For interactive quizzes, count the initial unanswered presentation and every later re-presentation after an answer or feedback as separate occurrences. Cite evidence from the matching occurrence's block; do not cover an earlier presentation only by citing a later repeated question. Classify eligible questions as Knowledge-checking or Instructional. Include `question`, `question_type`, and `concept_checked`.
- **Issues** (`issues`): Record supported factual, conceptual, calculation, procedural, reasoning, terminology, or language problems in tutor content. Do not speculate; state the issue and a clear correction or alternative in `explanation`.

Use the exact output fields and values in the supplied response schema. Include only its required `segment_id` and quote evidence fields; do not add other IDs, offsets, ratings, commentary, or extra fields. Do not annotate student statements as tutor evidence.

teach me about newton's laws of motion

Newton's 3 Laws of Motion 🚀

Newton's Laws of Motion explain why objects move, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction.

They were developed by Isaac Newton and are the foundation of classical physics.

We'll learn each law with simple explanations, real-life examples, and a quick quiz at the end!

1. Newton's First Law — The Law of Inertia

An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at a constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force.

In simpler words:

  • A soccer ball won't move until you kick it.

  • A moving ball will keep moving unless something slows it down or changes its direction.

  • Friction and air resistance are forces that can slow things down.

Real-life example: When a car suddenly stops, your body tends to keep moving forward. That's why seatbelts are important!

Remember

Inertia means an object's resistance to changes in its velocity. More mass means more inertia.

2. Newton's Second Law — Force = Mass × Acceleration

This law explains how forces change an object's motion.

nzherald.co.nz

F = ma

Net Force = Mass × Acceleration

Here's what the letters mean:

  • F = Net force, measured in newtons (N)

  • m = Mass, measured in kilograms (kg)

  • a = Acceleration, measured in m/s²

Example: Imagine pushing an empty shopping cart versus a full one. The full cart requires more force to accelerate at the same rate because it has more mass.

Try changing the force and mass

Mass

5 kg

Net force

20 N

Resulting acceleration

4.00 m/s²

20 ÷ 5 = 4.00

Try increasing the mass while keeping the force the same. What happens to acceleration?

Key idea: More net force means more acceleration. More mass means less acceleration for the same net force.

3. Newton's Third Law — Action and Reaction

For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

launchphotography.com

Imagine a rocket launching into space.

  • The rocket pushes exhaust gases downward.

  • The gases push the rocket upward with an equal and opposite force.

  • This helps the rocket accelerate upward.

Another example is jumping. Your feet push the ground downward, and the ground pushes you upward.

Important: The two forces act on different objects, so they don't cancel each other out on one object.

Quick summary

Law

Main idea

Example

Test your knowledge! 🧠

QUESTION 1 OF 3

The easiest way to remember Newton's laws is:

1st Law: Objects resist changes in motion.

2nd Law: Forces cause acceleration.

3rd Law: Forces always come in pairs.

Once you understand these three ideas, you can explain everything from kicking a soccer ball to launching a spacecraft!

is it applicable even in space?

Yes! Newton's three laws of motion apply in space too! 🚀 In fact, space is one of the best places to understand them because there's very little air resistance or friction.

1. First Law — Inertia in Space

Imagine an astronaut floating in space who throws a ball.

  • The ball keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed if no net force acts on it.

  • Unlike on Earth, there's almost no air resistance to slow it down.

  • However, gravity from nearby planets, stars, and other objects can change its motion.

Fun fact: A spacecraft can coast through space without continuously firing its engines!

2. Second Law — F = ma in Space

space.com

Suppose an astronaut pushes a 10 kg object with a net force of 20 N.

Using Newton's second law:

a=Fm=2010=2 m/s2a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{20}{10}=2\text{ m/s}^2a=mF​=1020​=2 m/s2

The object accelerates at 2 m/s², just as it would on Earth under the same net force.

3. Third Law — Rockets Work in Space

spacevoyageventures.com

A common misconception is that rockets need air to push against.

They don't!

  • The rocket pushes exhaust gases backward.

  • The exhaust gases push the rocket forward.

  • This works even in the vacuum of space!

That's Newton's third law.

But there's one important detail!

Newton's laws are extremely accurate for ordinary spacecraft motion, but they have limitations.

At speeds close to the speed of light, we need Einstein's special relativity. For extremely strong gravity or very precise calculations, we may need general relativity.

Quick question for you 🧠

If an astronaut throws a ball in deep space, far from significant gravitational influences, what will happen to it?

A. It will gradually slow down and stop.

B. It will continue moving at constant velocity.

C. It will accelerate forever.

so does the object not stop at all if it is in motion because of inertia?

Exactly! 🎯 You've understood Newton's First Law!

An object in motion will keep moving forever at the same speed and in the same direction, as long as no net external force acts on it.

This happens because of inertia.

🚀 Imagine this experiment in space

You're an astronaut floating in deep space, far away from planets and stars.

You throw a ball at 10 m/s.

Assuming no external forces act on it:

Time after throwing

Speed

1 second

10 m/s

1 minute

10 m/s

1 hour

10 m/s

1 year

10 m/s

1 million years

10 m/s

The ball would continue moving at 10 m/s indefinitely!

But why do objects stop on Earth?

Imagine rolling a ball across the floor.

It eventually stops because of:

  • Friction between the ball and the floor.

  • Air resistance opposing its motion.

Without these forces (or any other net force), the ball would continue moving.

Here's something interesting! 🧠

Inertia doesn't actually push an object forward.

An object doesn't need a force to keep moving. It only needs a net force to change its velocity.

That's one of Newton's most important discoveries.

Let me challenge you with a question!

If a spaceship is traveling through deep space at 20,000 km/h and suddenly turns off its engines, what happens?

A. It immediately stops.

B. It gradually slows down.

C. It keeps moving at 20,000 km/h.

Replace only listed invalid indices; do not remove or regenerate other entries. Additions may contain only missing Concepts heading annotations. Reuse the same hierarchy path when a missing heading repeats an existing node, and do not add a heading already covered by a replacement. Return empty arrays when appropriate.

For `repair_mode: full`, return the complete annotations object in the normal schema. Recheck segment IDs, exact canonical quotes, heading-only Concept evidence, table-header-only evidence, and example status. Return only valid JSON, without Markdown or commentary.
